barriers.description: Hospital privacy and security requirements forced removal of cancer-specific content and prevented in-app note storage, constraining designers' ability to provide tailored features.
barriers.justification: This organizational constraint limited designers' ability to specify user requirements and address the holistic user experience by preventing features that required higher privacy (eg, diagnosis-specific content or personal notes), thereby constraining design decisions and potential iterations.
barriers.reference_excerpt: For example, one security concern was that if the intervention mentioned diagnoses (eg, cancer), this could compromise user privacy. Another option was to completely avoid the word cancer and any cancer-specific information in the app. Based on user input and security recommendations, it was decided to choose the second option and not include diagnosis-specific information.

barriers.description: Usability testing included a limited number of participants, restricting the designers' ability to robustly evaluate the prototype with diverse users.
barriers.justification: The small sample size constrained the evaluation workload and the team's capacity to manage evolving user understanding and to reliably integrate feedback across varied user groups.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Second, the usability testing included a limited number of participants, which is, however, not uncommon for iterative design processes [49].

barriers.description: Usability testing covered all functionalities but did not test all content sentences, leaving portions of content unvalidated with users.
barriers.justification: By not evaluating all content, designers were limited in their ability to fully evaluate designs and integrate feedback for content-level refinement, potentially missing issues affecting comprehension and engagement.
barriers.reference_excerpt: First, usability testing involved all functionalities but not all content sentences.

barriers.description: Participant recruitment relied on a convenience sample from hospital and social-media invitations, introducing selection bias among interviewed users.
barriers.justification: This recruitment approach limited the designers' ability to manage comprehensive user understanding and to ensure requirements represented the broader target population, constraining specification of user requirements and iteration priorities.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Cancer survivors participating in the user interviews responded to hospital or social media-related invitations and represented a sample of convenience, which can introduce selection bias.
